lead: This unit explains what an embedded system is, how such systems are classified, and the trade-offs a designer must settle before writing any code. It then opens the box: the hardware platform and software layers, the processor family you pick (microprocessor, microcontroller, DSP or SoC), the instruction set and memory organisation inside it, and the memory chips around it. After this unit you can read a product's requirement list, sketch its block diagram, choose a processor and memory set, and defend the choice with numbers.
about: This unit builds the vocabulary the rest of the subject uses. Chapter 1.1 defines an embedded system and separates it from a general-purpose computer. Chapter 1.2 sorts embedded systems into classes, and 1.3 turns those classes into measurable design metrics and the trade-offs behind them. Chapter 1.4 opens the box and shows the hardware platform and the layered software stack sitting on it. Chapter 1.5 helps you pick the processor — microprocessor, microcontroller, DSP or SoC — and 1.6 goes one level deeper into instruction set style (RISC/CISC) and memory organisation (Harvard/von Neumann). Chapter 1.7 closes with memory technology, because choosing flash, SRAM or DRAM fixes both the cost and the speed of the final design.

chapters.idea: An embedded system is a computer built inside a larger product to do one dedicated job, usually under real-time limits — it is not a small laptop.
chapters.depth: Definition: a computer hidden inside a larger device, running fixed firmware for a dedicated function, normally with real-time constraints and limits on memory, power and cost. Some syllabi say 'dedicated computer' or 'special-purpose computer'. Contrast with a general-purpose computer, where the user chooses the program. Characteristics: single function; tight hardware-software coupling; constrained memory, power, cost and size; reactive to inputs; often real-time; little or no user interface; firmware fixed at manufacture; long life and high reliability. Application domains, one example each: consumer (washing machine), automotive (engine control unit, ABS), medical (glucometer, pacemaker), telecom (router, set-top box), industrial (PLC, motor drive), banking (POS terminal, ATVM ticket machine), defence (missile seeker), utilities (electricity meter). Define sensor (converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal: LM35 for temperature, LDR for light, IR sensor for presence) and actuator (converts an electrical signal into physical action: DC motor, relay, solenoid valve, buzzer). One line of history: the Apollo guidance computer is an early example; today a ₹2,000 appliance carries a microcontroller. Name IoT, edge AI and low-power design as current trends, without detail.

figure.title: Parts of an embedded system
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain: sensor, signal conditioning, processor with memory, driver, actuator, with the processor box marking the computing part.

chapters.example: Decide which of these are embedded systems and give input → process → output for each: (a) laptop, (b) IRCTC ATVM ticket machine, (c) washing machine, (d) digital electricity meter, (e) UPI soundbox. Answers: (b), (c), (d), (e) are embedded — each is a computer inside a product with one job. ATVM: card and key presses → fare and seat logic → printed ticket. Washing machine: water-level and knob settings → wash-cycle program → motor and valve. Meter: voltage and current samples → energy accumulation → LCD and pulse output. Soundbox: payment message over the network → decode and check → speaker announcement. (a) is general-purpose: the user installs whatever software they like.
chapters.trap: Small size does not make a system embedded — a laptop is general-purpose however portable. Also 'real-time' does not mean 'fast'; it means a deadline is met.
chapters.leave: Classification to 1.2, metrics to 1.3, architecture detail to 1.4. Timers, interrupts, DMA and serial ports are only named here — Unit 3 teaches them. RTOS ideas belong to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Embedded systems are sorted on three independent axes: complexity, timing requirement, and form or connectivity.
chapters.depth: Axis 1, functional complexity and word size: small (8-bit, no OS, a few KB of flash — washing machine, toy), medium (16- or 32-bit, small RTOS — router, printer), large or sophisticated (32/64-bit SoC, embedded Linux or Android — car infotainment, smartphone). Some syllabi label these small/medium/large, others type A/B/C. Axis 2, real-time requirement: hard (a missed deadline is a system failure — airbag, ABS), firm (a late result is worthless but harmless — a dropped video frame), soft (a late result is still useful — a sluggish display refresh). Axis 3, form and connectivity: standalone, distributed or networked (many nodes sharing a bus or a wireless link), and mobile. Add classification by generation (4-, 8-, 16-, 32-bit) and by implementation platform (MCU-based, DSP-based, FPGA-based, SoC-based). Stress that complexity class and timing class are independent: an 8-bit microwave controller is hard real-time and a 64-bit tablet is soft.

figure.title: Three ways to classify
figure.aria: A tree with the root 'Embedded systems' splitting into three branches — complexity, timing and form — each with two or three named leaves.

chapters.example: Classify each device on both the complexity axis and the timing axis, and give the reason: (a) digital wristwatch, (b) ABS brake controller with a 5 ms control loop, (c) washing machine controller, (d) 4G router in a bank branch, (e) airbag controller that must fire within 20 ms of impact detection. Answers: (a) small, soft — a late display update is harmless; (b) medium, hard — a missed 5 ms loop loses braking control; (c) small, soft — a slow spin is only annoying; (d) large, soft and networked — many flows, best-effort delivery; (e) medium, hard — a 20 ms miss is a safety failure.
chapters.trap: Students rank hard real-time systems as 'large and fast'. A tiny 8-bit controller can be hard real-time while a 64-bit tablet is soft. The two axes answer different questions.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for the definition and example devices.
chapters.leave: The metrics each class implies to 1.3. Wireless and network protocols to Unit 4. Scheduling of hard and soft tasks to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Every design decision is judged on measurable metrics, and improving one metric usually costs another.
chapters.depth: Define each figure of merit with its unit. Unit cost = NRE / quantity + recurring cost, where NRE (non-recurring engineering) is the one-time design cost in rupees and recurring cost is parts plus assembly per unit. Time-to-market: months of delay, and the revenue lost in that window. Performance: throughput (operations per second), latency (time from input to output, in ms or µs), and deadline margin. Power and energy: dynamic power P = C·V²·f plus static leakage, where C is switched capacitance in farads, V the supply in volts, f the clock in hertz; battery life = energy / average power. Also size, weight, flexibility (how easily the function can change in the field), reliability, safety, security, maintainability and correctness. Then the design challenges: choosing the hardware-software split; meeting deadlines with the cheapest legal part; fitting code in flash and data in RAM; the power budget of a battery device; picking a processor before good compilers exist; testing a board with no screen or keyboard; field firmware upgrade; safety and security. State the trade-off rule — of cost, performance and power you can usually improve two. Mention that rising IC design cost (higher NRE) makes platform choice a business decision, not only a technical one.

figure.title: Unit cost falls with quantity, but the crossover depends on NRE
figure.aria: Two falling curves of unit cost against quantity; the high-NRE curve starts far above the low-NRE curve and crosses below it at 800 units.

chapters.example: Design A uses an SoC: NRE ₹5,00,000, recurring cost ₹300 per unit. Design B uses an FPGA: NRE ₹1,00,000, recurring cost ₹800 per unit. (a) Unit cost of each at 200 units. (b) Unit cost of each at 2,000 units. (c) The quantity at which they are equal. Answers: (a) A = 500000/200 + 300 = 2500 + 300 = ₹2,800; B = 100000/200 + 800 = 500 + 800 = ₹1,300 — B wins. (b) A = 500000/2000 + 300 = 250 + 300 = ₹550; B = 100000/2000 + 800 = 50 + 800 = ₹850 — A wins. (c) Set 500000/q + 300 = 100000/q + 800, so 400000/q = 500 and q = 800 units: below 800 units build on the FPGA, above 800 build the SoC.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to divide NRE by quantity, or comparing unit costs at quantity 1. NRE is paid once; unit cost is NRE spread over the whole production run plus the recurring cost.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.1 and 1.2 — the device class decides which metrics dominate.
chapters.leave: How the architecture realises these metrics to 1.4 and 1.5. Low-power design techniques to Unit 6. Development tool cost and the design flow to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: An embedded system is a hardware platform plus a layered software stack, and where you draw the hardware-software line is a design decision.
chapters.depth: Hardware architecture: processor core, program memory (flash), data memory (SRAM), clock oscillator, reset circuit, power supply with brown-out detection, peripherals (timers, UART, ADC, GPIO), the internal bus connecting them, and the sensors, actuators and connectors outside. Software architecture, bottom to top: hardware; device drivers or board support package (BSP) that touch registers; middleware (RTOS or scheduler, protocol stacks, file system, libraries); application software that holds the product's logic. Name the jobs of each layer and the rule that a layer talks only to the layer below through a defined interface. Mention application software versus communication software as two side-by-side blocks above middleware. Name reset types briefly (power-on reset, external reset button, watchdog reset, brown-out reset) — Unit 3 and Unit 5 take them further. Name the wiring ideas the syllabus lists: a pull-up resistor holds a line at logic high when nothing drives it, a pull-down holds it at logic low, and a high-Z (floating) pin is not a logic level at all, which is why unused inputs get a pull-up or pull-down. Development environment (IDE, compiler, simulator, emulator, MCU internals) — one sentence each, pointing to Unit 6.

figure.title: Software layers over hardware
figure.aria: A four-layer stack: application software on top, then middleware, then device drivers, then hardware at the bottom.

chapters.example: Draw the hardware blocks and assign the software layers for a smart electricity meter built from: energy-measurement IC, 32-bit MCU, 64 KB flash, 8 KB SRAM, real-time clock, LCD, IR port, UART to a modem, and a push button with a 10 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V. Answer: hardware blocks = measurement IC → MCU (flash, SRAM, RTC, UART, LCD driver) → LCD, IR port, modem, with the oscillator, reset circuit and 3.3 V supply feeding the MCU. Software: application = tariff and billing logic; middleware = meter-reading protocol and RTC-based scheduling; BSP = drivers for the measurement IC, UART, LCD and IR port. The button line reads logic high through the pull-up and is pulled to 0 V when pressed; the pull-up stops the line floating when the button is open.
chapters.trap: Calling the RTOS 'the application', or drawing a hardware block diagram with no clock, reset and power. Also: a pull-up resistor sets a known logic high; high-Z is not a logic level.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.1 to 1.3 for the device, its class and the metrics the architecture must meet.
chapters.leave: Timer, interrupt, DMA and serial-port internals plus GPIO detail to Unit 3. Protocols to Unit 4. RTOS services to Unit 5. IDE, compiler, simulator and emulator to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The processor is chosen by the arithmetic pattern, memory need, power budget and production volume of the workload — microprocessor, microcontroller, DSP and SoC are different answers to different workloads.
chapters.depth: Microprocessor: a CPU on its own chip with address and data buses brought out, needing external RAM, ROM and I/O; the 8086 is the classic teaching example, an ARM Cortex-A in a phone is the modern one. Microcontroller (MCU): CPU, flash, SRAM, timers, serial ports, ADC and GPIO on one die, so a small system needs no extra chips; 8051, PIC16 and ARM Cortex-M are the standard families. DSP: a processor tuned for multiply-accumulate — a hardware MAC unit, separate program and data buses (Harvard), a barrel shifter, saturating arithmetic and address generators for circular buffers; used in audio, video, motor control; a 'digital signal controller' is an MCU with DSP features added. SoC: a whole system on one die — CPU cores, GPU, memory controller, radio, peripherals; the ASIC route gives low unit cost at very high NRE, the FPGA route gives zero NRE and short time-to-market at higher unit cost per board. Give a choosing table with columns: workload arithmetic, compute needed (MIPS or MMAC/s), memory, power, unit volume, tool support.

chapters.example: An audio filter computes a 256-tap FIR filter at a sampling rate of 48 kHz. (a) How many multiply-accumulate operations per second? (b) Can a 30 MHz MCU with no hardware MAC run it if each MAC costs 4 cycles? (c) What minimum DSP clock is needed at 1 MAC per cycle? Answers: (a) 256 × 48,000 = 12,288,000 ≈ 12.3 M MAC/s. (b) 12.288 M × 4 = 49.15 M cycles/s, so 49.15 MHz is needed — the 30 MHz MCU is too slow, at 30 MHz it manages only 30/4 = 7.5 M MAC/s. (c) ≥ 12.288 MHz; pick 25 MHz for margin and for the rest of the code. This is why a DSP or a DSP-enhanced MCU is the right choice for audio.
chapters.trap: Comparing a DSP and an MCU on MIPS alone. The DSP does one MAC per cycle in hardware while the MCU needs several cycles plus several instructions per MAC; convert both to MMAC/s before comparing.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.4 for the hardware blocks, chapter 1.3 for cost, power and time-to-market.
chapters.leave: 8051, PIC and ARM register-level architecture to Unit 2. Peripheral programming to Unit 3. FPGA and GPU design flows to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Instruction set style (RISC or CISC) and memory organisation (Harvard or von Neumann) are two separate design choices that set how fast and how costly a processor is.
chapters.depth: CISC: complex instructions of variable length, many addressing modes, memory operands allowed inside arithmetic instructions, microcode decoding, few instructions per high-level statement; examples 8086 and 8051. RISC: fixed-length instructions, load-store design (only load and store touch memory), many general registers, most instructions in one cycle, pipeline friendly, more instructions per high-level statement but each is simple; examples ARM, MIPS, RISC-V. Give a comparison table: instruction size, addressing modes, cycles per instruction, code size, register count, pipeline, decoding. von Neumann: one memory and one bus carrying both instructions and data; simple and cheap, code and data share the same space, but the single bus limits throughput (the von Neumann bottleneck). Harvard: separate program and data memories with separate buses, so one instruction fetch and one data access happen in the same clock cycle; costs more pins and forces separate address spaces; used by most MCUs and DSPs. Modified Harvard: separate instruction and data caches over one main memory, as in ARM application processors. Add the independence rule with one sentence of proof: the 8051 is CISC with Harvard memory.

figure.title: Harvard memory organisation
figure.aria: Program memory on the left feeds the CPU over its own instruction bus while the CPU reads and writes data memory on the right over a separate data bus.

chapters.example: A CPU has a 20 MHz bus and every 16-bit transfer takes one bus cycle. (a) Bus cycle time? (b) Time to fetch a 16-bit instruction and then read a 16-bit operand on a von Neumann machine? (c) The same on a Harvard machine? (d) Speedup? Answers: (a) 1/20 MHz = 50 ns. (b) One shared bus, so 50 + 50 = 100 ns. (c) Two separate buses, so the fetch and the operand read overlap: 50 ns. (d) Speedup = 100/50 = 2×, so at the same clock the Harvard machine retires up to 20 M such instructions per second against 10 M for the von Neumann machine.
chapters.trap: Treating RISC and Harvard as the same thing, or CISC as automatically slow. Pipeline depth, clock speed and memory buses decide speed; the two choices are independent.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.5 — you can only compare RISC/CISC and Harvard/von Neumann once you know which chip class you are looking at.
chapters.leave: 8051 and ARM register sets, addressing modes, pipelines and assembly language to Unit 2. Bus protocols such as AMBA, AHB and APB to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Memory is chosen by four questions — volatile or not, writable in the field or not, how fast, and how many bits per rupee — and each answer lands in a fixed place in the memory map.
chapters.depth: Volatile means the contents vanish when power is removed. ROM family: mask ROM (pattern fixed at the factory, cheapest at volume), PROM (programmed once by the user), EPROM (erased by ultraviolet light through a quartz window), EEPROM (erased and written electrically, byte by byte, limited endurance), OTP (one-time programmable). Flash: EEPROM-like but erased in blocks or sectors rather than bytes, so a write is erase-then-program; NOR flash allows random access and execute-in-place and holds code; NAND flash is page-addressed, denser and cheaper and holds bulk data, but needs bad-block management and a file system. Endurance for flash is typically 10⁴ to 10⁵ erase cycles per block, which rules out logging every millisecond into on-chip flash. SRAM: six-transistor cell, holds data while powered, no refresh, fast, low density, costly per bit; used for registers, on-chip RAM and caches. DRAM: one transistor plus one capacitor per cell, needs periodic refresh, dense and cheap, slower; SDRAM and DDR are clock-synchronised versions used as main memory. Give the memory map of a typical MCU: flash at address 0 because the reset vector lives there, on-chip SRAM above it, peripheral registers at fixed addresses. Choosing rule: code in flash, variables and stack in SRAM, large frame buffers in DRAM, logs and firmware images in NAND or an SD card.

figure.title: The embedded memory hierarchy
figure.aria: A five-level stack from registers at the top down through SRAM, flash, DRAM and NAND flash, marked faster and costlier at the top and slower and cheaper at the bottom.

chapters.example: A battery-powered data logger has 12 KB of program code and 1 KB of constant lookup tables. It samples a sensor every 1 ms, 4 bytes per sample, and must keep 8 hours of samples while powered off. Its MCU has 64 KB flash and 8 KB SRAM. (a) Flash needed for code and tables? (b) Bytes produced in 8 hours? (c) Can the log live in on-chip memory? Answers: (a) 12 + 1 = 13 KB, so 64 KB flash is enough. (b) samples = 1000 per second × 3600 s × 8 = 28,800,000; bytes = 28,800,000 × 4 = 115,200,000 bytes ≈ 115 MB ≈ 110 MiB. (c) No — 8 KB SRAM holds about 2,000 samples, and 110 MiB of on-chip flash writes would wear the block out, so the log goes to NAND flash or an SD card and only a small RAM buffer is kept.
chapters.trap: Writing flash byte by byte like EEPROM — flash must erase a whole block before programming it. Also, SRAM is volatile even though it holds data without refresh, and EPROM is erased by UV light, not electrically.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.4 for where memory sits in the hardware block diagram, chapter 1.6 for the separate program and data memories of a Harvard machine.
chapters.leave: Cache and pipeline behaviour to Unit 2. External memory interfacing and bus timing to Unit 3 and Unit 4. File systems and memory management inside an OS to Unit 5.
